"Kingdom come" is an old English expression that refers to the afterlife — the world that comes after death, often imagined as heaven or God's eternal kingdom. When people use this idiom, they are essentially pointing to a place or time beyond this world — somewhere far away, unreachable, or permanent.

The phrase is almost never used literally today. Instead, it appears in two main everyday situations:

1. To describe total destruction or death — meaning something or someone has been completely obliterated, sent "to the other world."

2. To describe an endless, almost infinite amount of time — meaning "forever" or "until the end of time."

To truly understand any idiom, you must know where it was born. This one has a very specific and famous origin.

"Kingdom come" is taken directly from The Lord's Prayer, one of the most well-known prayers in Christianity. In the King James Bible (1611), the prayer includes the line:

"Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven."

In this prayer, "Thy kingdom" refers to God's kingdom — which is heaven, or paradise. "Come" is a wish, a prayer that God's kingdom will arrive — meaning the end of the earthly world and the beginning of God's eternal reign.

So the phrase "kingdom come" quite literally means "the arrival of God's kingdom" — a divine, eternal place that exists beyond ordinary life and death.

Over time, ordinary English speakers began borrowing this phrase from the prayer and using it in everyday speech — but in a looser, more dramatic way. They stopped thinking about it religiously and started using it simply to mean "the next world," "death," "eternity," or "a place very far from here."
How the Idiom Is Used in Sentences

Meaning 1: Death, Destruction, or Being Sent to the Afterlife

This is the most common use. When you say someone or something was sent, blown, or blasted "to kingdom come," you mean they were completely destroyed or killed, as if they were hurled into another world entirely.

Examples:

  • "One wrong move and that bomb could blow us all to kingdom come."
    → One mistake and we'll all be killed/blown to pieces.
  • "The explosion blasted the old building to kingdom come."
    → The explosion completely destroyed the building.
  • "If he touches my car again, I'll send him to kingdom come."
    → (Dramatic and sometimes humorous exaggeration) I will destroy him.

Notice that this usage is very dramatic and often involves exaggeration (called hyperbole). People use it for strong effect, not to be taken completely literally. You'll often see it in action movies, thriller novels, and casual dramatic speech.

Meaning 2: Forever, Until the End of Time

The second usage carries the idea of eternity — because "kingdom come" is the end of all time, waiting "until kingdom come" means waiting indefinitely, or an absurdly long time.

Examples:

  • "We could argue about this till kingdom come and still not agree."
    → We could argue forever and it wouldn't change anything.
  • "She'll wait for him until kingdom come if she has to."
    → She'll wait forever, no matter how long it takes.
  • "The government could delay this decision till kingdom come."
    → The government could keep delaying this forever.

In this meaning, the phrase works like saying "forever," "until the end of days," or "for all eternity." It is often used with a tone of frustration, exaggeration, or hopelessness.
The Most Common Fixed Phrases to Know

The idiom almost always appears inside a few specific word combinations. These are the patterns you'll see most often:

  • "Blow/blast/send [someone or something] to kingdom come" → to completely destroy
  • "Till/until kingdom come" → forever, endlessly
  • "Wait till kingdom come" → to wait an impossibly long time
  • "Gone to kingdom come" → dead, destroyed, or completely gone

This idiom is informal and colloquial. You would use it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Novels and movies (especially action, drama, or thrillers)
  • Journalism for dramatic effect
  • Humor and sarcasm

You would not normally use it in:

  • Formal academic writing
  • Official documents
  • Professional business communication

It can be serious or humorous depending on context. If someone says "that explosion sent the car to kingdom come," they might be describing something genuinely terrifying. But if someone says "my mom will nag me about this till kingdom come," they're being funny and exaggerating for effect.

It carries a hint of the old and dramatic. Because the phrase comes from Biblical language, it has a slightly old-fashioned, theatrical feel to it. This is part of why writers and speakers like using it — it makes a sentence sound more vivid and powerful.

It is not offensive or inappropriate. Even though it has religious roots, the idiom is now so deeply embedded in general English that it isn't considered disrespectful to religion. It's simply a part of everyday English expression.
Quick Summary to Lock It In

Literal originFrom the Lord's Prayer — "Thy kingdom come" = the arrival of God's heaven
Core ideaThe afterlife, eternity, or the end of the world
Meaning 1To be completely destroyed or killed ("blown to kingdom come")
Meaning 2Forever, for an endless time ("till kingdom come")
ToneInformal, dramatic, sometimes humorous
RegisterCasual speech, fiction, journalism — not formal writing

The next time you hear "kingdom come," simply ask yourself: is the speaker talking about something being destroyed, or something lasting forever? Those are the only two paths this idiom ever takes — and now you know exactly how to read both of them.
